title: WPMS/2627/2013 of SMT. KIRAN Vs SMT. NIRMAL KUMARI

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition No.2627 of 2013 (M/S)
Smt. Kiran and another ...Petitioners
Versus
Smt. Nirmal Kumari and others ...Respondents
Present: Mr. Siddhartha Singh, Advocate for the petitioners.
Mr. Nikhil Singhal, Advocate for the respondents.
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
 (Via Video Conferencing)
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. It is a tenant's petition, wherein the tenant has put in challenge
to the impugned judgment dated 28.05.2011, as was passed by the Judge
Small Causes Court/Civil Judge (Sr. Div.), Hardwar in S.C.C. Case No.13
of 2002, Smt. Nirmal Kumari and another vs. Ram Prakash through L.Rs.,
which, on a challenge being given by the petitioners in a revision under
Section 25 of the Act; being S.C.C. Revision No.18 of 2011, Ram Prakash
Lrs. vs. Nirmal Kumari and others; which had ultimately, resulted into the
dismissal of the revision by the judgment dated 07.10.2013, and hence
apparently it seems that there were a concurrent finding of facts, which has
been recorded by the court below, while considering the S.C.C. Suit No.13
of 2002 which was preferred by respondents landlord for the purposes of
seeking an eviction and recovery of arrears of rent from the
tenants/petitioners, in the SCC Suit, which was thus instituted by the
respondents.

- 2 -
3. To be very précised and instead of elaborating, the findings,
which had been recorded on the merits of the matter, this Court is confining
its finding only to a limited extent,
(i) as to what impact and bearing would the provisions
contained under Section 20(4) of the Act No.13 of 1972 would
have, in the light of the subsequent acquisition of the property by
the tenant over an SCC suit, which was an issue and an aspect which
was agitated before the SCC court, but was not considered and no
finding has been recorded or returned by the revisional court on the
same, and
(ii) furthermore, on the impact as to what would be the scope of
interference of the revisional court with regards to the
implications of Order 15 Rule 5.
4. If the trial court's judgment is taken into consideration, the
point of determination, as it had been modulated by the said court has been
detailed with in para 5 of the judgment, which reads as under:-

5. Particularly a reference may be had to the issue no.7, which
was dealing with the issue of applicability of the Act and hence, it was
undisputedly held that the provisions of Act No.13 of 1972 was applicable
over the tenement in question. But for the impact of issue on Section 20(4);
issue no.6 was considered and it was an issue dealt with as to whether the
tenant would be entitled for the benefit of Section 20(4) of the Act or not?
But however, the learned trial court in its finding recorded on issue no.9 has
dealt with the impact of the subsequent acquisition of the property by the
defendants by virtue of the sale deed, which was referred therein as to be
Paper No.53 Ga, which was in consideration before the revisional court.
6. The learned trial court by the judgment dated 28.05.2011, had
considered the impact of the date of first hearing because according to the
argument extended by the counsel for the petitioners, the manner in which
the interpretation of deposit which had made on the first date of hearing,
has been given by the court below, it had been wrongly inferred, because
according to him the point of determination was framed by the trial court on
20.02.2003; though in this case, that even much prior to it i.e. framing of
point of determination, his tender of depositing of rent as was claimed in
the notice, which was issued under Section 106 of Transfer of Property Act,
was already remitted by the petitioners on 03.09.2002 and hence, the
argument of the counsel for the petitioners, is that the said interpretation,
which had been given, to the benefit of rejecting the notices for termination
of tenancy was wrongly interpreted by the court; and was not given to the
petitioners of terminating the tenancy, in the light of as to what would be

- 4 -
the implication and interpretation of the date of first hearing. However, the
issue no.9, when it was dealt with by the Court and also recorded a finding
that though it may not be quite an absolute finding, in relation to the
acquisition of the property, which was also one of the ambit which was
considered while interpreting the impact of the provisions contained under
Section 20(4) of the Act.
7. Be that as it may. However, this judgment of the learned trial
court, was ultimately put to challenge by the petitioners, in a SCC Revision
and the revisional court while dealing with this revision, has confined its
finding with regards to the implications contained under Section 15 Rule 5,
as made applicable, by the State amendment, which applied to the State of
U.P., and now in Uttarakhand also after its bifurcation in view of the
provisions contained under Section 87 of the Re Organization Act.
8. The argument of learned counsel for the petitioners, is that the
interpretation given by the courts to the impact of Order 15 Rule 5, with
regards to the continuance of deposit of rent, as it had been made is
perverse because according to him, his argument and case is that the rent
was continued to be paid; even during the proceedings of the case before
the court below, which has been argued to the contrary by the learned
counsel for the respondents/landlord his case was that in fact, after
31.08.2002, the petitioners/tenants had not remitted any rent and as such,
since there was a snapping of the remittance of rent after 31.08.2002, in that
eventuality, the striking of defence as contemplated under Order 15 Rule 5

- 5 -
of C.P.C. was rightly attracted by the revisional court. This Court is of the
view that so far as the aspect of striking of the defence is concerned under
Order 15 Rule 5, then the issue would be as to whether, it would also entail
empower the revisional jurisdiction, of venturing into the matter on its
merits, while deciding the revision itself, because it happens to be a
provision, which entails a consideration of both facts and evidence both and
rather a per the judicial precedents, it is a provision, which read to be in
parlance with the provisions contained under Section 96 of the Code of
Civil Procedure. Apart from it, if the revisional court's judgment, which is
impugned in the present writ petition, is taken into consideration, there is
no finding recorded in relation to the aspects of issue no.9, which was dealt
by the Judge, Small Causes, with regards to the impact of an acquisition of
the property by the petitioners/tenants during the pendency of the suit,
which was an issue dealt with by the learned trial court.
9. On that limited count itself that the revisional court has not
dealt with all the aspects, which were the subject matter of consideration
before the learned trial court; for eg.
(a) with regards to Order 20 Rule 4 i.e. the effect of deposit to be
made on the first date of hearing,
(b) also with regards, to as to what implication will 20(4) of the
Act, No.13 of 1972 would have with regards to the subsequent
acquisition of property by the tenants
(c) as to whether the implications of Order 15 Rule 5 of C.P.C.
striking of a defence, would itself entail deciding the revision itself

- 6 -
on its merit has not been appropriately dealt with by the revisional
court and as such, on that limited count itself, this writ petition is
partly allowed. The judgment of the revisional court dated
07.10.2013 is hereby quashed.
I. While upholding the judgment of the trial court, which will be
still a subject matter to be considered in a revision, which is in
pursuance to today's order, is directed to be decided on its own merit.
However, the revisional court will return its finding while
considering the aspect pertaining to Section 20 (4) of the Act i.e. the
deposit to be made on the first date of hearing.
II. The impact of Section 20(4) of the Act, once again with regards
to the effect of the acquisition of the property by the tenants at a later
stage.
III. As to what implications would the provisions of Order 15 Rule 5
will have over a revision, which itself entails a striking of a defence,
in an event of non remittance of continued rent during the pendency
of the proceedings.
10. Apart from above, the revisional court is directed to decide the
said revision exclusively on its own merits, within a period of six months
from the date of the receipt of certified copy of the judgment. Accordingly,
the writ petition partly succeeds. The matter is remanded to the revisional

- 7 -
court for its fresh decision. However, there will be no order as to cost.
 (Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.)
